query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy (for example, Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10 in at%), supplementing the alloy with an additional 10 at% Al and applying an optimized subsolvus aging treatment (tailored over a narrow temperature range, 725–775°C, for 4–6 hours) will promote the formation of a uniform dispersion of nanoscale, coherent B2 ordered Ti–Ni aluminide precipitates. This microstructural refinement will impede dislocation motion via coherency strain fields, thereby significantly enhancing high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to a baseline alloy that has been only homogenized and quenched.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, cast high-entropy alloy with primary constituents Ti and Ni, with composition approximately Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10 (at%), ensuring each element is within the 5–35 at% range.
generation.intervention: Introduce an additional 10 at% Al and perform a controlled subsolvus aging heat treatment. This involves first homogenizing the alloy at ~1200°C followed by a rapid quench, then applying a series of aging treatments (e.g., at temperatures between 725°C and 775°C for 4–6 hours in an inert atmosphere) to induce the formation of nanoscale coherent B2 ordered precipitates.
generation.conditions: The alloy is homogenized at approximately 1200°C and rapidly quenched. Aging treatments are performed within a narrow window (725–775°C for 4–6 hours) under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation and to maintain precipitate coherence. The intervention is designed to support mechanical performance up to 800°C.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed, nanoscale coherent B2 ordered Ti–Ni aluminide precipitates embedded within a disordered, Ti–Ni matrix.
generation.mechanism: The formation of nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates introduces local coherency strains that act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion. This precipitation strengthening mechanism is intended to retard dislocation glide and creep processes at elevated temperatures, thereby effectively enhancing high-temperature yield strength and extending creep rupture life.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized aging treatment should yield at least a 15–20% increase in high-temperature yield strength and improved creep rupture resistance (tests at 700–800°C) relative to a baseline alloy that is processed without the supplemental Al addition and optimized aging treatment.
generation.baseline: A similarly composed alloy (Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10) processed by homogenization at ~1200°C and quenching only, which remains as a homogeneous solid-solution without the beneficial nanoscale precipitation.
generation.boundary: The material composition adheres to the high-entropy alloy criteria (each element between 5–35 at%) and the aging treatment is confined to subsolvus conditions (725–775°C for 4–6 hours) to avoid formation of coarse, deleterious phases. The target operating temperature for improved performance is established at up to 800°C.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the exact aging parameters (temperature and time) that will reproducibly yield the targeted nanoscale and coherent precipitate morphology without transforming into unwanted brittle intermetallic phases. Iterative heat-treatment optimization and detailed microstructural characterization are necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with composition Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10. The control group will undergo homogenization at ~1200°C and quenching only. The experimental group will receive the additional 10 at% Al treatment and be subjected to the optimized aging treatments (systematically varied within 725–775°C for 4–6 hours). Perform detailed microstructural analysis (using TEM and XRD) to assess the presence, size, distribution, and coherency of the B2 precipitates, and carry out mechanical tests (high-temperature yield strength and creep rupture tests at 700–800°C).
measurements: TEM for precipitate morphology and size
XRD for phase identification and coherence assessment
Creep rupture life measurements at temperatures up to 800°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if either (a) the optimized aging treatment fails to produce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates, or (b) the alloy with the intervention does not exhibit at least a 15–20% improvement in high-temperature yield strength and enhanced creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy.

proposals.material_system: A high-entropy alloy with primary constituents Ti and Ni, for example formulated as Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10 (at%), which meets the 5–35 at% requirement for each element.
proposals.intervention: Introduce 10 at% Al and perform a controlled subsolvus aging heat treatment after homogenization to promote the nucleation and growth of nanometer‐scale, coherent B2 ordered precipitates (a titanium–nickel–aluminide phase) within the disordered solid-solution matrix.
proposals.conditions: Process the as-cast alloy via homogenization at ~1200°C followed by a rapid quench. Then, age at 750°C for 4–6 hours under an inert atmosphere (to prevent oxidation), targeting an operating temperature range up to 800°C for mechanical performance.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates distributed uniformly in the Ti–Ni solid-solution matrix
proposals.mechanism: The precipitates introduce coherency strains and act as obstacles to dislocation motion. This precipitation strengthening mechanism is expected to retard high-temperature creep and enhance yield strength by impeding dislocation glide and recovery processes relative to the homogeneous baseline alloy.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy processed without the aging treatment (or without the Al addition that triggers B2 formation), the intervention alloy should exhibit significantly improved high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance—quantitatively, an increase in yield strength by at least 15–20% and improved creep rupture life in tests at 700–800°C.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By focusing on the development of a precipitation-strengthened microstructure in an alloy where both Ti and Ni are the primary constituents, this hypothesis directly targets the open question of how to improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties. The approach leverages well-documented precipitation strengthening mechanisms (similar to those in nickel-based superalloys and titanium aluminides) in a novel compositional regime, thereby extending prior work where Ti and Ni were only minor additions.

critiques.addresses_problem: The direction directly targets the open question by proposing a precipitation strengthening mechanism in a high-entropy alloy where Ti and Ni are primary constituents. It introduces a testable intervention (Al addition and aging treatment) that should enhance elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
critiques.constraints: The proposed composition (e.g., Ti35Ni35Al10Cr10Mo10) respects the high-entropy alloy definition (each element within 5–35 at%) and uses Ti and Ni as the primary constituents. The aging treatment and operating conditions (aging at 750°C for 4–6 hours with performance expected up to 800°C) are stated in clear boundaries.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound, relying on the formation of nanoscale coherent B2 ordered precipitates, which are known to introduce coherency strains and hinder dislocation motion. This approach mirrors established precipitation strengthening mechanisms in related alloy systems.
critiques.feasibility: The intervention is feasible using standard metallurgical processing methods such as homogenization, rapid quenching, and subsolvus aging. However, the precise control of precipitate size and distribution might be challenging.
critiques.evidence: The hypothesis leverages supporting evidence from analogous systems (nickel-based superalloys and titanium aluminides) where precipitation strengthening has been successfully exploited. Although no specific literature record IDs are provided, the mechanism is well-documented in the literature.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the targeted B2 ordered phase may not form with the desired nanoscale, coherent morphology or could evolve into unwanted brittle intermetallics under the proposed processing conditions.
critiques.fix: Include a more detailed heat-treatment optimization plan (e.g., a series of aging temperatures and times) and a microstructural characterization protocol (using TEM and XRD) to ensure the precipitates remain nanoscale and coherent without forming deleterious phases.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly addresses the open question by proposing a precipitation strengthening mechanism in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy, using an Al addition and subsolvus aging treatment to form nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates. The critic’s suggestion to add a more detailed heat-treatment optimization plan and robust microstructural characterization protocol (e.g., via TEM and XRD) is straightforward to incorporate, strengthening the feasibility and controlling risks of unwanted brittle phase formation. Thus, we adopt direction A with this fix.
